summary: Reproduces a memorandum issued on 2 July 1987 by the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Command, Control, Communications, and Intelligence to the Director of the Defense Communications Agency, on the DoD position on Open Systems Interconnection protocols. It is distributed for information only and replaces RFC 945.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a copy of an official letter from the US Defense Department about how it planned to treat the OSI family of networking rules.

subtitle: A US Defense Department memo that let OSI protocols stand beside the DoD protocols as experimental co-standards.

tldr.problem: Protocols based on the ISO Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model were progressing quickly, and the DoD needed a policy on how they related to the DoD protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adopts the OSI message handling and file transfer protocols, with their underlying protocols as defined in GOSIP, as experimental co-standards to the matching DoD protocols, and asks agencies to take specific follow-up actions.
tldr.outcome: It states an intent to make OSI a full co-standard once GOSIP is a Federal Information Processing Standard, and later the sole mandatory suite, with interoperation with DoD protocols kept.

sections.title: A Reproduced Memorandum
sections.content:
RFC 1039 reproduces a memorandum issued on 2-JUL-87 from the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Command, Control, Communications, and Intelligence to the Director of the Defense Communications Agency (DCA). It is distributed for information only.

The memo says there had been rapid progress in protocols based on the ISO model for Open Systems Interconnection (OSI). The Government OSI Profile (GOSIP), dated 22 April 1987, has enough information to specify and acquire interoperable vendor implementations of OSI message handling and file transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: The letter says the second family of rules had grown up enough that the Defense Department needed to decide how to treat it.

sections.title: The Policy Change
sections.content:
Because of GOSIP, the earlier policy on host-to-host protocols (the USDR&E memo of 23 March 1982) is modified. The OSI message handling and file transfer protocols, with their underlying protocols as defined in GOSIP, are adopted as experimental co-standards to the DoD protocols that provide similar services (MIL-STDs 1777, 1778, 1780 and 1781).

They may be specified in addition to, in lieu of, or as an optional alternative to the DoD protocols. They are experimental because of limited operational experience and the limited operational, testing and security environment defined in GOSIP. Services and agencies choosing them should evaluate those factors and be ready for the complications of new technology.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rules could be used next to the old ones, but only as a trial, because nobody had much experience with them yet.

sections.title: The Planned Transition
sections.content:
The memo intends to adopt the OSI protocols as a full co-standard when GOSIP is formally approved as a Federal Information Processing Standard. Two years after that, the OSI protocols would become the sole mandatory interoperable protocol suite. A capability to interoperate with the DoD protocols would be provided for the expected life of systems supporting them.

The final implementation details are to be provided later in a DoD Directive.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan was to treat the two families as equals first, and later to make the new one the main one while keeping a way to talk to the old one.

sections.title: Requested Actions
sections.content:
The DCA Director, as DoD Executive Agent for Data Communications Protocol Standards, is asked to publish the DoD-OSI Interoperability and Transition Plan by November 1987. Experimental interoperability of message handling and file transfer is to be provided by March 1988, and a limited operational capability by January 1989.

The DCA Director is also asked to join the Corporation for Open Systems (COS) as the DoD representative and to coordinate Service and agency participation in OSI standards groups. The Director of the National Security Agency is asked to make sure the Secure Data Network Systems program can supply the security extensions that GOSIP lists as future work. Services and agencies are asked to share their early implementation experience.
sections.plainLanguage: The letter also gave homework: write a plan, join an industry group, work on security, and share what you learn.
